subject: anatomy
title: Glossopharyngeal, Vagus, Accessory, and Hypoglossal Nerves

steps.tx: Cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII form the caudal group of cranial nerves, arising from the medulla oblongata and innervating visceral, pharyngeal, and cervical structures. Cranial nerves IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), and XI (accessory) exit the skull together through the intermediate and posterior compartments of the **jugular foramen**, closely related to the internal jugular vein.
steps.say: Arising from the medulla, cranial nerves nine, ten, eleven, and twelve govern vital bulbar functions. Nerves nine, ten, and eleven exit together through the jugular foramen.

vis.alt: Anatomical schematic showing caudal cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII emerging from the medulla oblongata
vis.caption: Anatomical trajectories of the lower cranial nerves emerging from the skull base into the neck. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) is the nerve of the third pharyngeal arch. It provides motor supply to a single solitary muscle: the stylopharyngeus. Sensory modalities are diverse: it supplies general and special taste sensation to the posterior third of the tongue, sensory supply to the **oropharynx** and palatine tonsil, and baroreceptor sensory input from the carotid sinus.
steps.say: Nerve of the third arch, the glossopharyngeal innervates only one muscle: stylopharyngeus. It conveys taste and touch from the posterior tongue and mediates carotid sinus reflexes.

rows: Elevates pharynx and larynx during swallowing
Secretomotor innervation via tympanic and lesser petrosal nerves
Posterior 1/3 of tongue, tonsil, pharynx, middle ear
Afferent sensory limb of the pharyngeal gag reflex
Baroreceptor blood pressure and chemoreceptor oxygen monitoring

steps.tx: The pharyngeal gag reflex tests the functional integrity of cranial nerves IX and X. Touching the mucosal wall of the oropharynx, palatine tonsillar pillar, or posterior tongue triggers bilateral pharyngeal contraction and retching. The sensory afferent limb of the **gag reflex** is mediated entirely by the glossopharyngeal nerve, while the motor efferent limb is carried by the vagus nerve.
steps.say: The gag reflex tests bulbar function. Touching the oropharynx fires glossopharyngeal sensory afferents, driving bilateral vagal motor pharyngeal contractions.

nodes.label: Mucosal Touch (Spatula touches posterior pharyngeal wall or tonsillar pillar)
Sensory Afferent Limb (Glossopharyngeal nerve CN IX carries impulses to solitary tract nucleus)
Central Synaptic Relay (Interneurons project bilaterally to nucleus ambiguus)
Motor Efferent Limb (Vagus nerve CN X stimulates pharyngeal constrictor spasm and gagging)

steps.tx: The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) is the longest cranial nerve, possessing the most extensive body distribution. Exiting the jugular foramen, it possesses a superior (jugular) and inferior (nodose) ganglion. Descending vertically within the **carotid sheath** between the internal jugular vein and carotid arteries, it supplies motor branches to all muscles of the pharynx, larynx, and palate (with noted single exceptions).
steps.say: The vagus nerve descends vertically within the carotid sheath between the artery and vein. It supplies all muscles of the pharynx, larynx, and soft palate, with three single exceptions.

left.title: Vagal Innervation Exceptions
points: Tensor veli palatini: Supplied by mandibular nerve (V3)
Cricothyroid: Supplied by external laryngeal nerve (X)
All other pharyngeal and palatal muscles supplied by vagus

right.title: Parasympathetic Autonomic Viscera
points: Heart: Bradycardia and decreased conduction velocity
Foregut & Midgut: Peristalsis up to distal transverse colon
Abdominal plexuses: Celiac, mesenteric, renal networks

steps.tx: The accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) possesses two distinct components: a cranial root and a spinal root. The cranial root arises from the nucleus ambiguus, briefly joining the spinal root before transferring entirely to the vagus nerve to form the **pharyngeal plexus**. The spinal root arises from C1-C5 anterior horn motor neurons, ascending through foramen magnum to innervate sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
steps.say: The accessory nerve has cranial and spinal roots. The cranial root merges with the vagus, while the spinal root ascends from C1-C5 to innervate sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.

rows: Exits jugular foramen, merges into vagal nerve trunk
Distributed via pharyngeal and laryngeal branches of vagus
C1 to C5 anterior horn spinal cord
Ascends through foramen magnum into posterior fossa
Traverses jugular foramen to supply sternocleidomastoid and trapezius

steps.tx: Testing of the spinal accessory nerve examines sternocleidomastoid and trapezius function. To test the right sternocleidomastoid, the patient is instructed to turn the head forcefully to the left against the examiner's resisting hand, while the muscle belly is inspected. To test the **trapezius muscle**, the patient shrugs both shoulders upward against manual downward resistance.
steps.say: Turning the head to the opposite side tests sternocleidomastoid, while shrugging the shoulders upward against resistance tests trapezius. Weakness confirms an accessory nerve lesion.

nodes.label: Sternocleidomastoid Testing (Patient turns chin to opposite side against resistance)
Trapezius Testing (Patient elevates shoulders upward against downward hand pressure)
Unilateral CN XI Deficit (Weak contralateral head turning and marked ipsilateral shoulder droop)

steps.tx: The hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII) is a purely somatic motor nerve arising from the hypoglossal nucleus in the dorsal medulla. It emerges from the anterolateral sulcus between the pyramid and the olive, exiting the skull via the **hypoglossal canal**. It descends in the neck, hooks around the occipital artery, and crosses the hyoglossus to supply all tongue muscles except palatoglossus.
steps.say: Emerging between the medullary pyramid and olive, the hypoglossal nerve exits through the hypoglossal canal. It supplies all intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus.

vis.alt: Anatomical schematic tracing the course of the hypoglossal nerve crossing the carotid bifurcation and hyoglossus
vis.caption: Surgical relations of the hypoglossal nerve crossing the external carotid branches in the neck. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Jugular foramen syndrome (Vernet syndrome) results from skull base fractures, glomus jugulare tumors, or schwannomas compressing the jugular foramen. It presents with combined ipsilateral paralysis of cranial nerves **nine, ten, and eleven**: loss of taste and sensation on the posterior tongue (IX), vocal cord and palatal paralysis (X), and sternocleidomastoid and trapezius weakness with shoulder droop (XI).
steps.say: Vernet syndrome involves cranial nerves nine, ten, and eleven at the jugular foramen. Patients present with dysphagia, vocal cord paralysis, uvular deviation, and shoulder droop.

cols: Loss of Function in Vernet Syndrome
rows: Loss of posterior tongue sensation, loss of gag reflex
Absence of pharyngeal contraction on touched side
Paralysis of soft palate, pharynx, and vocal cord
Uvula deviates to normal side; hoarseness and aspiration
Shoulder droop; inability to shrug or turn head to opposite side
If canal involved, adds tongue hemiparalysis
Protruded tongue deviates to affected side with hemilingual atrophy
